title: The impact of exogenous estrogen on the male body (from a broscientist perspective)
summary: Personal-experience take (explicitly not study-based) on dietary estrogen. Men need some estrogen; naturals stay balanced, but sensitivity to food estrogens (soy, dairy, red meat, plastics) varies. NH says cutting milk and red meat slimmed his love handles at the same bodyweight, and that raw garlic and onions give him great pumps and vascularity.

claims.claim: This is based on personal experience, not verified science.
Men need some estrogen: without it mood becomes erratic, joints aren't lubricated and recovery suffers. Naturals' hormones stay balanced, avoiding both gyno and low-estrogen side effects.
Being natural doesn't guarantee an optimal ratio; you can still have too much estrogen or too little testosterone.
Phytoestrogens, mammal estrogens and xenoestrogens from plastic do have an effect in his view, but its size depends on genetics and receptor sensitivity.

Most studies find soy isn't feminising, but they test normal consumption, not overconsumption; there are cases of men who lost male characteristics after soy replaced much of their protein, while others drink a gallon of soy milk a day with no issue.
Cow's milk contains a lot of estrogen too; for him it didn't cause gyno but increased fat and water retention around the love handles and waist.
At 240 lbs and 6 ft he was fat with huge love handles; after a crash cut to 205 lbs he had a six-pack but the love handles remained.
About four months ago he gave up milk and most red meat; at the same bodyweight and calories, his love handles slimmed noticeably as if they no longer retained water.
If you're lean and vascular but keep stubborn love handles, try cutting dairy and see what happens.
Changing his estrogen intake didn't noticeably change his strength or muscle size.
Raw garlic, onions and capers are said to boost testosterone; he hasn't tested his levels, but raw garlic gives him insane pumps and more vascularity without cutting.
He will never be a channel that makes diagrams of what the science says; he shares his own experience.
